content: Module 4 Evaluation Method o Why evaluation is essential in NLP o Benchmark datasets and gold-standard annotations o Why annotation reliability matters o Inter-annotator agreement o Observed agreement, expected agreement, and Cohen’s Kappa o The confusion matrix: TP , FP, FN, TN o Precision, recall, and F1-score o When accuracy can be misleading o Micro, macro, and weighted averages o Entity-level evaluation for NER Why Do We Evaluate NLP Systems? ● Evaluation tells us how well a system is performing. ● Users care about whether a system is useful for a task. ● Developers care about whether a system is improving over time. ● Evaluation supports: ○ comparison ○ debugging ○ model selection ○ scientific reporting Benchmark Data and Gold Standards ● Performance evaluation is often based on benchmark datasets. ● These datasets contain: ○ inputs ○ gold-standard labels ○ a fixed evaluation protocol ● Gold standards are usually created by human annotators following annotation guidelines. ● Reliable evaluation depends on reliable annotation. Inter-Annotator Agreement ● Human annotations are not always identical. ● Different annotators may interpret a guideline differently. ● Inter-annotator agreement measures how consistently humans label the same data. ● High agreement suggests the task and the guidelines are clearer and

more reliable. Observed Agreement: 𝑃 𝑎 ● Observed agreement is the proportion of cases on which annotators agree. ● Example: ○ two annotators label 10 items ○ they agree on 7 items ● Then: ○ 𝑃 𝑎 = 7/10 = 0.70 ● Observed agreement does not correct for chance agreement. Expected Agreement:

𝑃 𝑒 ● Expected agreement estimates how much agreement would happen by chance. ● Suppose: ○ Annotator A assigns Positive to 6/10 items and Negative to 4/10 ○ Annotator B assigns Positive to 5/10 items and Negative to 5/10 ● Then: ○ chance agreement on Positive = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30 ○ chance agreement on Negative = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20 ● So:

○ 𝑃 𝑒 = 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.50 Cohen’s Kappa ● Cohen’s Kappa corrects observed agreement for chance agreement. ● Formula: ○ 𝐾 = 𝑃 𝑎 −𝑃 𝑒 1−𝑃 𝑒 ● Using the previous example: ○ 𝑃 𝑎 = 0.70 ○ 𝑃 𝑒 = 0.50 ○ 𝐾 = 0.70 − 0.50 / 1 − 0.50 = 0.40

● Kappa is more informative than raw agreement alone. Scoring Precision: fraction of annotated items that are correct Recall: fraction of correct items that are annotated Confusion matrix: Correct Not correct Annotated True positive (TP) False positive (FP) Not annotated False negative (FN) True negative (TN) Precision = TP / (TP+FP) Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

Blue stars Not blue stars True Positives: False Positives: False Negatives: True Negatives: Precision = TP / (TP+FP) = 5 / (5 + 2) = 5 / 7 = 0.714 Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 5 / (5 + 1) = 5 / 6 = 0.833 F-score (a.k.a. F-measure, F1-score) Weighted harmonic mean
Fβ = (β2 + 1)PR/β2P+R Usually balanced F1 measure is used, where β=1 F1 = 2PR/(P+R)

Harmonic mean is a more conservative average (truer picture) F-score vs Arithmetic Mean P = 0.714 R = 0.833 Arithmetic Mean: (0.714 + 0.833) / 2 = 0.774 F-score: 2 * 0.714 * 0.833 / (0.714 + 0.833) = 0.769 F-score vs Arithmetic Mean
P = 1 R = 0.15 Arithmetic Mean: (1 + 0.15) / 2 = 0.575 F-score: 2 * 1 * 0.15 / (1 + 0.15) = 0.261 What about Accuracy? Measure of all correctly identified cases
Acc = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)) Suitable if all classes are equally important. What if not? Example: Hate vs Neutral Use F-score Multiple Categories:

Option 1: Macro-averaging -- Simply get the average PPerson+Location = (0.94+0.87)/2 = 0.91 RPerson+Location = (0.70+0.91)/2 = 0.81 F1Person+Location = (2*0.91*0.81)/(0.91+0.81) = 0.86 Category TPs FPs FNs Precision Recall

Option 2: Micro-averaging -- Pool together the TPs, FPs and FNs PPerson+Location = (78+20)/((78+20)+(5+3)) = 0.92 RPerson+Location = (78+20)/((78+20)+(33+2)) = 0.74 F1Person+Location = (2*0.92*0.74)/(0.92+0.74) = 0.82 Category TPs FPs FNs Precision Recall

Category TPs FPs FNs Precision Recall Person 78 5 33 0.94 0.70 Location 20 3 2 0.87 0.91 Confusion Matrix for evaluating automated predictions ● For automated systems, evaluation often starts with a confusion matrix. ● For a positive class: ○ TP: predicted positive, actually positive ○ FP: predicted positive, actually negative ○ FN: predicted negative, actually positive ○ TN: predicted negative, actually negative

● Many common metrics are derived from these four counts. Positive class (Response) Negative class (Response) Positive class (Reference) True Positives (TP) False Negatives (FN) Negative class (Reference) False Positives (FP) True Negatives (TN) Worked NER Example: Counting Entities ● Tokens: ○ Dr | Maya | Chen | joined | Acme | Labs | in | Bristol | . ● Gold tags: ○ B-PER I-PER I-PER O B-ORG I-ORG O B-LOC O ● Predicted tags: ○ B-PER I-PER O O B-ORG I-ORG O O O ● Entity counts: ○ PER: TP = 0, FP = 1, FN = 1

○ ORG: TP = 1, FP = 0, FN = 0 ○ LOC: TP = 0, FP = 0, FN = 1 ● The person prediction is wrong because the predicted span is incomplete. Gold entities ● Maya Chen = PER ● Acme Labs = ORG ● Bristol = LOC
Predicted entities ● Maya Chen = PER ● Acme = ORG ● Bristol = LOC Counts ● PER: TP = 1, FP = 0, FN = 0 ● ORG:

TP = 0, FP = 1, FN = 1 ● LOC: TP = 1, FP = 0, FN = 0 Key point: A partially correct span does not count as a true positive. Precision and Recall ● Precision asks: ○ Of the items predicted as positive, how many are correct? ○ 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 = 𝑇𝑃/ 𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑃
● Recall asks: ○ Of the truly positive items, how many did the system find? ○ 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 = 𝑇𝑃/ 𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁
● Precision and recall capture different aspects of performance. The F1 Score ● F1 combines precision and recall using the harmonic mean. ● Formula: ○ 𝐹1 = 2𝑃𝑅 𝑃+𝑅

● F1 is high only when both precision and recall are high. ● It is often preferred when the positive class is important and class balance is uneven. Worked Example: Computing F1 ● Suppose a spam detector produces: ○ TP = 18 ○ FP = 6 ○ FN = 9 ● Then:
○ Precision = 18 / (18 + 6) = 0.75 ○ Recall = 18 / (18 + 9) = 0.67 ○ F1 = 2 × 0.75 × 0.67/ 0.75 + 0.67 ≈0.71 ● This shows the full calculation from counts to F1.
When Accuracy Can Mislead ● Accuracy measures the proportion of all correct decisions. ● Formula: ○ 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦 = 𝑇𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 / 𝑇𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 + 𝐹𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁
● Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced datasets. ● Example: ○ if 95% of items are negative, always predicting negative gives 95% accuracy ○ but recall for the positive class is 0

● In such cases, F1 is often more informative. Micro, Macro, and Weighted Averages ● For multi-class problems, we often report combined performance. ● Macro average: ○ compute the metric for each class ○ then average across classes equally ● Micro average:

○ pool all TP , FP , and FN first ○ then compute the metric once ● Weighted average: ○ average class-level metrics using class frequency as weights ● The choice affects how strongly rare classes influence the final score.
Worked Example: Micro-Averaged F1 for NER Using the previous example: ○ PER: TP = 1, FP = 0, FN = 0 ○ ORG:
TP = 0, FP = 1, FN = 1 ○ LOC: TP = 1, FP = 0, FN = 0 Now pool all counts across entity types:

○ Total TP = 2 ○ Total FP = 1 ○ Total FN = 1 ○ 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑚𝑖𝑐𝑟𝑜 = 2+1 = 0.667 ○ 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙𝑚𝑖𝑐𝑟𝑜 = 2+1 = 0.667 ○ 𝐹1𝑚𝑖𝑐𝑟𝑜 = 2×0.667×0.667 0.667+0.667 = 0.667 ● Interpretation: Micro-averaging gives one overall score after combining all entity decisions across categories. Module 5.

Open Information Extraction oWhat Open Information Extraction is oHow OpenIE differs from predefined relation extraction o A brief view of classical and neural OpenIE approaches What Is Open Information Extraction? ● Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) extracts relational facts from text without relying on a fixed predefined schema. ● Input: ○ raw sentences or documents ● Output: ○ relation tuples such as (argument, relation, argument)

● OpenIE aims to turn unstructured text into machine-readable knowledge. What an OpenIE Extraction Looks Like ● Sentence: ○ Albert Einstein published the theory of relativity in 1915. ● Example extraction: ○ (Albert Einstein; published; the theory of relativity) ○ (Albert Einstein; published in; 1915)

● OpenIE relies heavily on earlier NLP steps: ○ POS tagging ○ parsing ○ entity recognition A Short View of OpenIE Methods and Limits ● Classical methods used: ○ patterns ○ dependency structure ○ clause splitting

● Later work introduced supervised and neural approaches. ● Common challenges include: ○ ambiguity ○ synonymy ○ coreference ○ trustworthiness of extracted facts ● In this module, OpenIE is a compact application case rather than the
main assessment focus.
